### **1.  Introduction & Executive Summary** 

###### **1.1 Introduction** 

Following our last 3-Year Silver Forecast (released on 17th February), silver entered an almost straight line rally.  With the silver price approaching its 1980’s peak of $50 in late April, the white metal had posted an increase of almost 60% during the first four months of this year, dwarfing the returns of most commodities and equity indices over the same period. 

Nevertheless, this upward trend came to an abrupt end in early May when silver suffered its largest weekly decline (one of 27%) for more than three decades. Much of the correction was due to profit taking from investors who had bought the metal at much lower prices.  The process was exacerbated by several hikes in margin requirements on silver by the CME group, which unsurprisingly caused many lev

eraged traders to make a quick move to exit. It is of note that, despite heavy technical selling, prices soon found firm support in the low $30s, reflecting bargain hunting by investors showing continued interest in the white metal. Essential to this is ongoing uncertainty over world economic growth, rising inflation fears coupled with worries regarding fiat currencies. For instance, several European countries including Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain have continued to faced troubles managing their debt so far this year. Meanwhile, an unexpected announcement by Standard & Poors on 19th April that it would downgrade the US government’s debt from stable to negative certainly reduced the dollar’s appeal, which subsequently dropped to a 25-month low of $1.49/€ in early May. Possibly one of the more significant influences on market sentiment in the second half of this year will come from continued loose monetary policy in the major industrialised countries, particularly in the United States.  Although QE2 is expected to end this month, the Fed’s chairman Bernanke has already signalled that the US central bank is in no rush to scale back its support for the economy.  Concern about inflation will also continue to be at the forefront of investors’ minds, as many look at rising energy and food prices as a lead indicator of future inflation or a weakening of the purchasing power of the dollar. 

Although we do not rule out a $50 plus silver price later this year, we believe this is less likely to occur. Unlike gold where investment demand is more based on medium to long term views, investor interest in silver has been much speculatively driven.  As such, investors could quickly liquidate their long positions if certain targets are achieved and therefore prices are vulnerable to any change in investor sentiment. 

As we expect the silver price to rally later this year, we forecast the full year average will reach a new alltime-high of the $36.30 in 2011 under our Base Case scenario (weighted with a 50% possibility). 

Moving to next year, we expect the aforementioned positive factors to remain broadly in place.  While the Fed may start to tighten its monetary policy next year, any initial rise in interest rates will be a very gradual process.  In addition, after a rally in the commodity prices this year, inflation fears could grow further, which should encourage continued investment inflows into the silver market.  However, at some point in 2012, our base case expectation is that the long bull run in silver (and gold) prices should come to an end. The subsequent slide back in prices could prove quite slight to begin with but could then accelerate, with the average price then falling to $28.70 in 2013. 

It is of note that our price forecast for the 2011-13 period under all scenarios has been revised upward since the previous forecast, due to silver’s robust price performance so far this year as well as growing investment inflows into the market. 

We can also project two potential scenarios for the global economy very different to our Base Case. **Scenario B** (with a 30% probability) presents the most positive outlook for silver prices, with an investor-led bull market continuing throughout the forecast period.

Much of the above discussion has focused on the interplay between changes in the principal economic variables and investment demand. As mentioned previously, however, we do not subscribe to the view that price direction and level are determined by invest

ment alone.  An analysis of trends in the key supply/demand variables shows that these have played and will continue to play an important part in price determination, and their importance is assessed below. 

###### **1.2 Base Case Scenario** 

Looking first at the supply side, global mine production is expected to continue rising through to 2013.  Not only is 2011 forecast to see the most significant annual output gain in GFMS’ series, but in the space of two years close to 100 Moz will be added to the global total (comparing 2012 with 2010).  Overall, the industry will benefit from a strong project pipeline, with healthy precious metal prices (and a robust outlook for base metals) providing further impetus.  In particular, by-product gold mining will account for much of the growth, itself driven by a robust increase in Mexican supply.  In the base metals industry, the contribution will largely come from the lead/zinc sector, especially near the beginning of the forecast.  In contrast, 2013 will see a slowdown in the rate of growth in lead/zinc mining, as existing reserves decline in the face of a less robust project pipeline. 

Amendments to the mine production series since the February report are slight and occur in 2012-13.  The upward revision in each year largely follows a review of the Chinese series, together with a reassessment of Kazzinc’s operations. 

Turning to scrap supply, after peaking in 2010, the recycling of silver is forecast to decline through to 2013.  The downward trend is primarily due to lower industrial scrap coupled with an ongoing decline in recycling from the photographic sector, although losses will initially be partly offset by higher jewellery and silverware scrap.  It is of note that our scrap series has undergone a noticeable upward revision since February, reflecting a higher starting point in 2010. 

As with previous reports, we expect net producer hedging to provide 40 Moz of demand this year. 









However, as prices start to decline, the scope for further hedging will be very limited in 2012, with a return to net de-hedging expected in 2013. 

Net government sales have been revised upward compared with the previous forecast, due to higher than expected disposals from Russia in 2010. Nevertheless, we maintain of the view that the absolute level of sales will remain modest, accounting for only 1.4% of total supply over the 2011-13 period. 

Turning to the demand side, after a major rebound last year, growth in industrial fabrication is likely to slow down significantly to 9% this year, although its total should comfortably exceed the previous record.  While the Japanese earthquake has caused some near-term production disruption within the country as well as at many assembly plants elsewhere, we expect the bulk of losses to be offset by an end-year improvement. Thereafter, industrial fabrication is set to see further gains, leaving its total in 2013 some 12% higher than the 2011 figure.  Our current forecas

t is markedly higher than the previous forecast, mainly due to a substantial upward revision in the Chinese series. 

Despite higher prices, jewellery fabrication will continue rising this year.  Ongoing market penetration in the youth demographic and further substitution gains at the expense of gold in western countries are the main drivers behind this increase.  In addition, higher offtake in the latter part of the forecast should also be underpinned by falling prices and rising consumer spending.  In contrast, both silverware and photographic demand will drift lower this year and then remain low in 2012 and 2013, broadly in line with the long-term secular decline in these sectors. 

Higher fabrication for this year also stems from robust growth in demand for coins & medals, which will register another record high in 2011.  Although demand will start to wane from 2012 onwards, its overall level should remain elevated by historical standards. 

Overall, the supply and demand figures forecast show that the market will remain in surplus (as defined by the sum of mine production plus scrap less fabrication) over the next three years, which suggests that the silver price is vulnerable to a major correction. Nevertheless, given that the economic backdrop will remain generally favourable for investment demand for silver, we expect investors to fairly comfortably absorb the surplus metal over the forecast period.

###### **1.3 Alternative Scenarios** 

**Scenario B** for silver prices over the forecast period.  After more than doubling in 2011 to an average of $40.76, annual average prices advance to an impressive $46.95 and $54.75 in 2012 and 2013 respectively.  As discussed earlier, driving this rally is the highly inflationary environment forecast under this variant.  This view is premised on the assumption that the massive fiscal stimulus and dovish monetary policies adopted in many countries, especially in the United States, prove effective in spurring growth. 

There are also notable contrasts between the supply/ demand balance (excluding investment) in this scenario and that under the Base Case.  Firstly, total supply is forecast to see a more positive trend in Scenario B, with higher volumes expected from every element on the supply side, particularly scrap and net producer hedging.  As such, overall supply will rise by 2013 to 1,171.4 Moz, more than 100 Moz higher than in the Base Case.  Secondly, fabrication maintains a slightly faster pace of increase, on the back of higher industrial offtake coupled with rising coin demand. Even accounting for higher losses in the photographic and silverware sector, fabrication demand is still some 50 Moz above the Base Case in 2013.  Changes since February mainly comprise markedly higher scrap and notably greater industrial fabrication. 

**Scenario C** presents an environment in which silv

er prices suffer the greatest losses, with average prices expected in 2013 almost 40% below our forecast for this year. This bear market occurs within an almost non-existent inflationary environment brought about by sustained sluggishness in the global economy, reflecting the inability of fiscal and monetary policies to boost consumption and reflate consumer and asset prices. Although this investor-led bear market does see a hefty decline in prices, the outcome would be far worse if it were not for the support which is expected to emerge from other supply/demand developments over the period. One of the greatest relates to a return to net producer de-hedging in 2012 and 2013. This combined with more modest growth in mine production coupled with lower scrap will see total supply being capped below 1,040 Moz by 2013, 30 Moz under the Base Case. Turning to fabrication demand, despite lower world GDP growth, industrial demand for silver will continue to rise, albeit at a slower pace. As such, total fabrication less coins is estimated at an average level lower than 29 Moz below the Base Case in each forecast year. Despite more muted supply, the market surplus will remain substantial, with bargain hunting investors being expected to help absorb the surplus. As with the previous forecast, we expect to see a slowdown in world economic growth in 2011. In the developing world, where inflationary pressures have been growing, it is anticipated that monetary and fiscal authorities will adopt policies to moderate growth. Meanwhile, in the developed world this slower pace of economic growth is mainly a result of the unsustainability of government deficits, which have been crucial to the reflating of

the global economy over the past eighteen months. An integral part of this is the absence of further fiscal stimulus or, in some European countries, outright fiscal austerity measures in an attempt to avert, or manage, sovereign debt crises. ###### **9.2 Silverware** 

###### **9.2.1  Introduction** 

Demand for silverware has been in a secular decline for several years with global consumption last year at 50.3 Moz almost 60% below the peak recorded in 1997.  Much of the fall is attributable to cultural and social changes in India and a notable shift in purchasing habits from within the western world.  In India, demand was historically driven primarily through investment.  However, over the last decade, consumers have looked to bars and coins as a more dependable means of storing wealth as relentless undercarating had led to a lack of consumer confidence.  In the west, a move away from formal entertaining and offering silverware as a traditional wedding present, or special occasion gift, has seen other more modern alternatives win market share at the expense of silver.
